notes.meaning: The opening list traces ten generations from Adam down to Noah's father, Lamech. Cain and Abel are passed over so the record can follow the family line that led to Noah. God chose to preserve and guide this specific family line through primeval history.

Noah had three sons after whom the entire post-Flood world was repopulated. All three brothers are listed because all modern nations branch out from them. This reminds us that every person on earth shares a common ancestry.

These names trace the family of Japheth, whose descendants moved toward the coastlands and northern areas. Israel had little contact with these distant peoples during their early history, so their family tree is brief. God keeps record of every nation, showing that his care extends to the whole earth.

Ham's descendants settled across parts of Africa and the ancient Near East, becoming nations like Egypt, Libya, and Canaan. The family of Cush expanded into Arabia, establishing known trading peoples like Sheba and Dedan. These regions would later interact frequently with the people of God.

Nimrod stands out as a powerful ruler and hunter who established early cities. Traditional readers see him as a proud leader who lifted himself above others and ruled harshly. His life is a reminder that human ambition often leads to rebellion against God.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest that Nimrod's father was not Ham's son Cush, but came from a distinct Babylonian background.

notes.meaning: Mizraim is the forefather of Egypt and several neighboring tribal groups. The Casluhites and Caphtorites are listed here as the source of the Philistines, who would become Israel's long-standing rivals. God recorded the roots of the very nations Israel would encounter in later history.

Canaan's family tree includes Sidon, his firstborn, along with groups like the Hittites, Jebusites, and Amorites. These names describe peoples and tribes rather than only individual men. They settled the land that God later promised to Abraham and his descendants.

This list names additional Canaanite peoples, such as the Hivites and Arkites. Over time, several of these smaller groups blended with neighboring tribes and lost their distinct identities. Remembering their names shows that God knew every group that lived in the land before Israel arrived.

Shem's family includes the ancestors of the Persians, Assyrians, and Syrians. The final four names are Aram's sons, listed here with Shem's direct sons because the term sons can include grandsons. This line is central to Scripture because it leads directly to the covenant people.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars believe the phrase 'and the sons of Aram' accidentally dropped out of the Hebrew text during copying.

notes.meaning: The lineage continues through Arphaxad to Shelah, and from Shelah to Eber. Eber is recognized as the ancestor from whose name the word Hebrew comes. God was quietly preserving the specific family line that would carry his promises to the world.

Eber had two sons, Peleg and Joktan. Peleg was named for a division, which traditional readers understand as the scattering of nations and languages at the tower of Babel. It marks an important turning point when humanity spread across different lands.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some popular modern teachers argue that the division in Peleg's day refers to the physical splitting of the earth's continents rather than language groups.

notes.meaning: Joktan fathered many sons who settled regions across the Arabian peninsula. These verses list the first seven of his sons, including Hazarmaveth and Jerah. Their families grew into distinct tribes and settlements in the ancient East.

The remaining sons of Joktan complete the branch of Eber's family that settled in southern Arabia. Places like Ophir and Havilah later became famous in biblical history for their gold and wealth. This record shows how broadly Shem's family expanded after the division.

The record returns to Shem's main line, moving from Arphaxad through Peleg down to Reu. By repeating this chain, the writer narrows the focus away from side branches back to the chosen line. God steadily advanced his covenant plan through each generation.

The genealogy reaches from Serug to Terah, ending with Abram, whom God renamed Abraham. God called Abraham and gave him special promises to bless all nations through his family. This list connects every family on earth from the first man, Adam, to the father of the faithful.
